The water came at night, as it usually does. By the morning, the high street was a river and the river was a lake, and the people of the town stood on the hill by the church and watched their lives float past.

That was four years ago. Today, almost nothing about the place looks the same. Houses sit on stilts or on the ridge. The school has a roof garden that doubles as an evacuation point. The old bakery is a pump station.
“We stopped fighting the river,” the mayor told me, standing on a bridge that now rises and falls with the seasons. “We started asking it what it wanted.”

Engineers call this managed retreat, a phrase almost everyone in town hates. Residents prefer something simpler: moving up. Across Europe, dozens of communities are now watching to see whether it works.

The costs are real. Some families left and never came back. Others spent savings meant for retirement. But the town has not flooded since, and for the first time in a generation, the population is growing.
On my last evening, children were racing paper boats in the channel that runs beside the new market. It was, a teacher pointed out, the first time in years anyone had looked at the water and laughed.
